Thanksgiving Day-Mr. Oershaw

speakeroldname: Mr. F. W. GERSHAW (Medicine Hat) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the day to be observed hereafter for national Thanksgiving day shall be Armistice day, November 11th.
He said: This resolution is brought forward as a tribute and to do honour to those who served in the great war. This proposal did1 not come from the returned soldiers, but since it appeared on the order paper many branches of the Canadian Legion have expressed approval of it, and many resolutions have been passed by that body expressing such approval.
We have about eight or nine public holidays in Canada. We have set aside a day in memory of that great sovereign Queen Victoria, known as Victoria day. We have another day set aside to commemorate a great event in the history of our national life, Dominion day. This resolution asks that the day set aside as Armistice day shall have special importance. We hope that the day shall be called Armistice day, so that the significance of the armistice shall not be forgotten. We hope that the memory of that great event with all that it brought to those then living in the way of joy and sorrow, relief from tension and hope for the future, will never grow dim. I feel sure that this day will not be observed in such a way as would glorify war.
The armistice was signed at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of 1918, and at that time the horror and sadness of war was uppermost in the minds of all. It was felt that a war had been fought which would stop all future wars. If that sentiment and that feeling cam be projected! into the ceremonies which take place in the future, much can be done to perpetuate the will and desire for peace in. the hearts of the people.
Perhaps we have enough holidays at present, because the schools have found it difficult to keep open for two hundred days during the calendar year, and the request is made that Thanksgiving day shall be merged with and observed on Armistice day, November 11. Thanksgiving day is a proclaimed holiday; it does not refer to any great event in history. I understand they have no Thanksgiving day in England. In the United States, Thanksgiving day has been observed since the time of the Pilgrim fathers. It is a day of festivity. When the crops are gathered it is celebrated by the getting together of the people and 78594-6
their taking part in a few sports and other diversions. During the first winter the Pilgrim fathers were in America, many of their number died, but when the spring and summer came there seemed to be some hope for them and the first Thanksgiving day was celebrated about that time. During the revolution eight special days were set apart for thanksgiving in order to celebrate special victories or special deliverances from danger. Since the days of President Lincoln Thanksgiving day has been the last Thursday of November.
It is a family day, a day of returning home for religious services, and none of us would like to see those splendid things come to am end; but it is close to Christmas, which we observe in much the same way, and the day that is known as Armistice day can still be a day for family reunion.
In fact, in Canada Thanksgiving day has not always been celebrated in the fail of the year and has not always been celebrated because a generous harvest has been reaped. The first Thanksgiving day celebrated in Canada was on the 10th of January, 1799, because of the signal victory over our enemies and the manifold blessings which our kingdom had enjoyed. The next was held on August 12, 1802; the next on April 21, 1814, for the glorious victory over our enemies; the next on September 13, 1814, on account of the ending of the war in Europe, giving the dominions the blessings of peace. The next Thanksgiving day was in 1815, on account of the end of the war with the United States of America and the blessing and restoration of peace. The next was in 1816, because of the end of the war between Great Britain and France; the next in 1833, because of the cessation of the cholera plague; the next in 1834, on account of the quarantine of ships at Grosse Isle; the next in 1838, because of the termination of rebellion; the next in 1850, for the cessation of grievous disease; the next in 1856, for the restoration of peace with Russia; the next in 1859, for the abundant harvest and the continuance of peace, and the next in 1863, for the abundant harvest.
Since confederation, Thanksgiving day was observed on the 15th of April, 1872, for the restoration to health of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, and again on the 6th of November, 1879, for the blessing of a harvest. Since that time there has been an annual Thanksgiving day. No one wishes to do away with Thanksgiving day but we are most anxious that Armistice day shall be suitably celebrated in the years that are to come. I hope the house will pass this resolution and that its object will be attained. War is a

Thanksgiving Day-Mr. Neill
disaster; the greater the war, the greater the disaster, but if the lessons of war are to be learned from past experience, surely much will be gained by keeping these experiences before us and celebrating Armistice day in honour of those who deserve the honour.

Mr. Speaker, I have much pleasure in seconding and supporting this resolution. In order that the house may be fully informed of the situation, I may explain that in 1921 the Union government passed an act which is now chapter 9 of the revised statutes of 1927, the second section of which provides that:
The Monday in the week in which the eleventh day of November shall occur .... shall be a legal holiday and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of Armistice day.
The next section goes on to state that the holiday commonly called Thanksgiving day shall be proclaimed and observed on the same day. It is on that that this resolution rests. Experience has shown and the feeling of the returned men as expressed by their bodies is that Armistice day is very liable to be and is in process of being merged and forgotten in Thanksgiving day. One cannot very well conceive the permanency of a celebration which may be moved anywhere within a week. Can you picture Christmas day, if it fell on a Saturday, being observed, for instance, on the previous Monday? Yet that is the situation in this case. Armistice day, according to the law passed in 1921, is to be observed on the Monday of the week in which it falls. The object of this resolution is to reverse this situation and have Armistice day held on the eleventh day of November and Thanksgiving day on the same day if necessary.
I have under my hand a resolution passed by the Dominion convention of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. It is only a few words, and I will read it:
Resolved that whereas November 11th is a day sacred to all ex-service men-
I would like to emphasize -the point that in the opinion of returned men and indeed in that of all of us it should be a day sacred to all ex-service men.
and the date set apart by the federal government for observance is a day other than this date;
Be it resolved that this convention requests the federal government to amend the present act so that in unison with other parts of the English-speaking world Canadian citizens may be enabled to commemorate the actual day upon which the armistice was signed as a national memorial day, and substitute it for Thanksgiving day.

I have a number of other resolutions from various branches of the legion, mostly in the district which I represent, and I will briefly quote from one or two. One of them reads: We feel that this day should be set apart from any other holiday as Armistice day cannot come on any other date any more than Dominion day can be called Christmas.
This is another one:
Whereas Armistice day heretofore has been made subservient to Thanksgiving day-
That is the point they have taken, that Armistice day has been and is made subservient to Thanksgiving day.

this branch hereby resolves, and do pray that thanksgiving and Armistice day be annually celebrated on November 11th of each year.
Another one, after expresing the sentiments I have already read, goes further and says amongst other things:
Further, that the matter of the considering the advisability of arranging for Thanksgiving (lay to always be observed on Armistice day, be left to those in authority for due consideration.
In other words, they do not absolutely demand or ask that Thanksgiving day be held on the same day, but they do ask that Armistice day be held on the 11th of November.
I have several more telegrams along the same lines, but I will not read them.
Two objections have been raised against this change, and I will deal briefly with them before I sit down. One is that it would cause two holidays in one week, and that is calculated to be embarrassing to business people and to business interests. It is not necessary to have two holidays in the one week. It is quite possible, as I have suggested and as the resolution suggests, to have Thanksgiving on November 11. This would would do away with that objection. Besides, if necessary, Thanksgiving day could be held in October. It has been held in October before now and we are not particularly committed to holding it in November. Labour day comes in September; Thanksgiving day might well come in October and Armistice day on November 11, but that is a matter for the government to decide. That does away with the objection that we cannot afford to have two holidays in one week.
The other objection, which is one that is given great weight in some quarters, is that it is inconvenient for travelling men and those whose business takes them away from home to have t-he holiday on any other day than Monday. It also interferes perhaps with those living in a town who wish to visit their relatives or friends in the country for what is called a long week-end; unless Armistice day

Thanksgiving Day-Mr. Church
comes on a Monday that is prevented. It is undeniable that it would be more con' venient for travellers to have the holiday on Monday, but I would point this out: Thanksgiving day, Labour day, Victoria day, and these other days are intended to be public holidays, and to be for the convenience of those away from home and for those who wish to visit their friends, but Armistice day was not intended at all for that purpose. It was never designed or set apart as a public holiday for the convenience of those who wished to visit their homes or their friends. It was intended and designated-it was consecrated, I might say-to the memory of the men who died at the front and those who had the good fortune to come back, men equally gallant, equally brave, equally ready to take the risks of war, in order that the rest of the population, and especially the rising generation, who were mere children while the war was on, should be reminded of, and should be instructed in, so to speak, the reverence and the respect and the obligation we owe to these men who risked their all at that time. As the resolution of the Dominion Convention of the British Empire Service League says, it is a day sacred to ex-service men; it has nothing whatever to do with a week-end holiday, and therefore I submit that Armistice day should be observed as such. I would point out that in every other English-speaking country with which I am familiar, they observe Armistice day on November the 11th, and not on the previous Monday or on any other day.
Again the argument is used: After all, that is a mere matter of sentiment that should not be allowed to interfere with the convenience and material interests of the everyday workaday world. Well, a great poet once said that it w'as sentiment that ruled the world, and that is quite true. What would this world be without sentiment? Why do we spend large sums, both as nations and as individuals, for the relief of the sick and the poor and the destitute? Is it not from sentiment. from a spirit of charity and sympathy nd goodwill? What about the war memorials scattered throughout this country, which must in the aggregate cost an enormous sum? They were erected purely from sentiment, and from a worthy and proper sentiment. I do not think the argument is a good one that this is a matter of sentiment and should therefore be ignored. Think of the tombstones that dot this land. They are erected from a spirit of sentiment, and sentiment only.
I do not anticipate that there will be any serious opposition to this resolution passing the house. This house may be divided for 78594-6i
this purpose into two classes, those who went to the war and those who d:d not. I am sure that those who were at the war will appreciate the spirit of their comrades in asking for this change. It is even more incumbent upon those of us who did not go [DOT]to the war to see that the wishes of the men who were at the front are respected in this matter, and that they are granted this comparatively trivial change, which in the end will hurt no one, but will be paying to these men the respect and reverence to which they are entitled.

The action that was taken by parliament in setting aside a day for general thanksgiving was not taken without national reasons, and national reasons in a matter of this kind should be paramount. The religious bodies, trades organizations, military bodies and many other social organizations represented that the best day for thanksgiving was Monday, which would best meet the convenience of commercial travellers, and those attending the public and separate schools and collegiate institutes. It also meets the convenience of a very large number of employees in the urban and industrial centres whose only chance to get back to their homes in the country, owing to the existing railway rates, is for the weekend during which Thanksgiving day comes. In Ontario especially there is a very large urban population whose homes are in the rural parts of the province, and owing to the action of the railways in doing away with the prewar chea,p excursion tickets that existed before the war, these young people are able to get home only once or twice a year, at Thanksgiving and at Christmas. All along the shores of the St. Lawrence, lake Ontario and lake Erie, and in many cities and towns across the border, there are tens of thousands of Canadians -working away from their homes in the United States. In Detroit, for instance, which to-day is the third largest city in the United States, there are over 250,000 Canadians. These young people once in a while come back to their homes in this country for a week-end at Thanksgiving, and many of them have to stay in the United States, where they have been driven to get a job by the fiscal policy of this government, and they have to celebrate the American Thanksgiving day. From what I have seen of this agitation, I know it is the opinion that Monday is the best day from the standpoint of the religious bodies and from the standpoint of the military man. The military men can get off for the week-end, but they cannot get off on the eleventh, if it comes on a Wednesday, for instance, be-

Thanksgiving Day-Mr. Rinfret
cause their employers will not let them go. A big store like Eatons, for instance, employs almost 20,000 people, many of whom come from Ontario and some from the west, and they try to get home for the week-end on Thanksgiving day when it is on a Monday. I would urge that no change be made in a matter of this kind until proper representations have been made, first, from the provinces, second, from the municipalities and third, from the military organizations and religious and social bodies in this country. The present arrangement has been found to work very satisfactorily, and I have heard no complaint against it.

I desire to say only a few words on
this motion, which has been so ably presented by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), and commented upon quite fully by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). As Secretary of State, I have myself been the recipient of a large number of letters and resolutions covering practically the same ground.
There is no doubt that there is a fairly widespread desire in this Dominion that we celebrate Armistice day on the very day of its anniversary, that is on November 11th. In fact, there exists some confusion in the minds of a great number of people as to these two holidays, Armistice day and Thanksgiving day. Some people are under the impression that we celebrate Armistice day on Thanksgiving day, but that is a wrong impression. Just the reverse is the case. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has alluded to the statute. As it is very short I might clear the situation up by reading a few clauses which I have before me.	[DOT]
The act respecting Armistice day was passed in 1921 and is now chapter 9 of the revised statutes of 1927. Clause 2 deals with Armistice day, and clause 3 with Thanksgiving day. Clause 2 reads:
throughout Canada in each and every year the Monday in the week in which the eleventh day of November shall occur, being the day in the year one thousand nine hundred .'and eighteen on which the Great War was triumphantly concluded by an armistice, shall be a legal holiday and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of Armistice day.
Clause 3 reads as follows:
The holiday commonly called Thanksgiving day, being a day usually appointed in the month of October or November by proclamation as a day of general thanksgiving to Almighty God, shall whenever appointed be proclaimed and observed for and on Armistice day.

So it will be seen that we are commemorating Armistice day on the Monday of the week in which the 11th of November falls, and we are directed by this act to proclaim Thanksgiving day on the same day. So that practically the only change suggested in this resolution is that these two holidays, instead of being celebrated on the Monday of the week in which the 11th of November falls, shall be celebrated on November the 11th, whether that be a Saturday, a Sunday or a Monday. Apparently the only practical objection to the adoption of this resolution is the desire to have the holiday follow a Sunday in order to extend the time available for travel. This argument does not appeal very much to me. I think the sentimental reason for observing Armistice day on November 11 is of such a lofty character as entirely to outweigh any considerations of personal convenience. Speaking for myself, I may say that if the resolution should be pressed to a division I shall vote for it. But this does not appear to be a matter for government policy, and the government will be directed by the desire of the people as expressed by their representatives in this house. In the event of the motion being adopted I shall endeavour immediately to bring down an amendment to the act to give effect to the wishes of the house.

I
quite see, Mr. Speaker, that the present legislation leaves something to be desired, because it does by inference, if not directly, provide that the celebration of the original armistice be made subservient to the celebration of thanksgiving. However that may be, legislation or no legislation, the people of this country are still too regardful of what Armistice day means to celebrate it on any other day than November 11. Ever since 1918 they have continued to celebrate it in the most solemn and fitting way on November 11; they so celebrated it last year and they will do so again this year and in the years to come. I should be very sorry, Mr. Speaker, to see Armistice day degenerated into a public holiday in which the celebration of the armistice would play only a small part.
I do not care what you do with Thanksgiving day, but I do not believe there is any desire among our people that we should make a general play day or holiday of Armistice day. Have Thanksgiving on any day you like but on November 11. Let us continue to commemorate the conclusion of the war by the most impressive ceremony of a two-minute silence on the morning of the day in proud

Family Allowances-Mr. Letellier de St. Just
and loving memory of our glorious dead, and of their deeds, in a spirit of thankfulness that their lives were not given in vain.
Above all things, Mr. Speaker, I hope the members of this house will consider very seriously that the adoption of the proposed amendment would make the celebration of Armistice day subservient to what is one of the great days of football, travel and visits of a more or less convivial nature. Let us be very careful not to do anything to detract from the solemnity and sweetness of Armistice day as we have it now.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in complete agreement with the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary). I think that November 11 should be commemorated for the things that are sacred to that day, and that its objects should not be combined with those that are generally associated with Thanksgiving day. If we are to have a day of general thanksgiving for material prosperity, I suggest that that day be fixed for, say, the middle of October. Let us preserve Armistice day for its own special purposes. It is sacred to our returned soldiers, and it is sacred to the memory of those who gave their lives for Canada.
