The government of the day has no right to put this proposition over, this monument of folly the way they put over the change of status-without the will of the people.
Let me tell the Prime Minister of this country that titles automatically became abolished in this country by Canada's changed status. The judiciary of the superior courts of this country are no longer entitled to be addressed, "My Lord," or "Your Lordship." The Prime Minister of this country settled all that by this magnificient dream of our new status, by this business of making Canada a nation overnight. Canada a nation of titles, with no navy except a few small craft such as row boats, now locked up in a garage at Halifax? That is the country that wants to restore titles 1
I think this country has had enough of this kind of legislation. Is this all that parliament has to do? Are we assembled here to discuss academic questions of this kind, titles, and all that kind of thing? Canada won a new title at the League of Nations, if you please; we have a seat at the league now. The League of Nations is going to cost us more and more in the future than all other agencies put together, and you would be convinced of that if you would only read the Empire and English Review. It shows the mischief that this particular agency is doing. If this opposition wants to be a fighting opposition, it ought to be up and doing, instead of being a sort of Woodrow Wilson opposition discussing titles and that kind of vanity and conceit; for it is a case of "vanity, vanity, saith the preacher; all is vanity".
I am aware of no demand for this resolution. The Conservative party had a platform at Winnipeg, and they were afraid to mention in it what has been the main plank of their platform ever since we became a party, the very backbone of the Conservative platform, namely, the title "protection." This government is giving away the water-power resources of this country to gentlemen who occupy offices on St. James street. There is too much government from St. James street and too little from Ottawa. Here we have been assembled for nearly a week, and instead of our trying to help the struggling men, women and children in Wales by sending them one or two million dollars, or studying the problem of the national coal supply and perhaps bringing out coal from Wales, we are sitting here dis-
cussing academic questions of this kind. The lowly carpenter of Nazareth had no title.
Last session we had a discussion on the table of precedence in this country. If you read it in the red book, "The Parliamentary Companion," you will find what a lot of has-beens members of the House of Commons are. They are twenty-third on the list in the table of precedence and are preceded even by honorary colonels-and this although such a table is abolished by Canada's new status.
Five hundred thousand Canadians went overseas and fifty thousand of them he buried in France. If the plain title of "Mister" was good enough for them, that style of address and salutation should be quite good enough for the civilians who stayed at home and became war profiteers. I believe that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George would be far better occupying his time in getting the unemployed in his and other constituencies titles to jobs in their own land instead of having to go to the United States as they are forced to do now under our economic system.
One of the greatest prime ministers that Great Britain has ever had, Mr. Stanley Baldwin, is a commoner. He will rank as a greater than William Pitt. Joseph Chamberlain, who gave us the magnificent dream of an economic empire, was content to be a commoner; those great Liberals, John Bright and Gladstone, were commoners, and so were many others who stood for what they conceived to be the principles of liberalism. I submit that those who support titles are not true to those Liberal principles. This house should occupy itself in solving the great economic problems of the empire, trade, defence and migration, instead of frittering away its time on such a purely academic question as titles. Canada has earned the title of the greatest spendthrift nation of the world. In 1896 it took thirty-six million dollars to run this country; to-day it takes four hundred million dollars. In 1896 some of the provinces spent 5 millions; now they spend 57 millions. It would be far better to discuss vital economic problems than waste our time on titles.
If we adopt this resolution and appoint a committee, then automatically we adopt the principle of the resolution. Let those who are in favour of titles declare themselves now.
I see no reason for altering the decision come to by the house in 1919 when the argument for and against titles was stated at very great length. The only action we need take in regard to titles is to deal with one or two hereditary titles enjoyed by a small number

This is the first time that I was ever given five minutes extra. This resolution follows somewhat the form of the resolution of 1919, but goes a little further, if anything. Everybody respects the hon. membeT for St. Eawrence-St. George, he is one of the active members of the house, and has given a great part of his life to the service of his fellow-citizens, but notwithstanding that, on a matter of principle, I must differ with him on this resolution. Its purpose is to appoint a committee of eleven to further investigate. What? To investigate and report on the very same principle on which the committee of 1919 reported. At that time the Liberal party was very largely lined up against the title principle. In the debate at that time Mr. Michael Clark, the then member for Red Deer, made a very important speech covering the four corners of this resolution. He supported the principles of Liberalism. Mr. Nickle gave a history of titles from feudal days and pointed out that Canada being a democratic country did not want to retain this relic of feudalism. The mover of the resolution wants to have a special committee appointed, consisting of eleven members, to investigate and report upon the advisability, first, of qualifying the address to His Majesty the King. No doubt certain gentlemen are to qualify for certain titles.	I see the hon. member for East
Toronto (Mr. Ryekman); I do not see why he should not be made an honorary colonel. He is as much entitled to that distinction as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). Is it intended that this motion shall affect such decorations as are conferred by the
Knights of Pythias, the Knights of Columbus and the Black Knights of Ireland? This parliament has no power to interfere with decorations such as are worn on the twelfth of July or the seventeenth of March. The motion also suggests amending or rescinding the address to His Majesty the King. Let us see what that address asks of His Majesty.
